note: Years and authors checked by web search on 21 October 2026: Social market economy (1947, the book; the term first appeared in print in 1946), Market socialism (1938, the book), Islamic economics (1963), Buddhist economics (1966). The other entries are from memory and still need checking.

models.name: Gift economy
models.author: Marcel Mauss
models.core: Goods move as gifts that create obligations to give and to return; status, alliances and trust are built through exchange rather than through price.

models.name: Household and peasant economy
models.author: Alexander Chayanov
models.core: A family farm balances the work it can do against the needs of its household, so production serves consumption and not profit.
sources: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy (1925)

models.name: Redistributive economy
models.original: Trade and Market in the Early Empires
models.author: Karl Polanyi, Conrad Arensberg, Harry Pearson
models.core: A central authority collects goods as tribute or taxes, stores them and redistributes them to workers and officials, as in temples, palaces and tributary states.
sources: Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires (1957)

models.name: Slave economy
models.author: Plantation owners and colonial legislatures
models.core: Labour is extracted through the ownership of people; the enslaved are denied education and property, and output is sold through trade.

models.name: Feudalism
models.author: Carolingian administrators
models.core: Peasants owe labour services and rents to a lord in return for land, protection and justice; the manor is largely self-supplying.

models.name: Guild economy
models.author: Étienne Boileau (compiler)
models.core: Craft guilds regulate entry, training, quality and prices; masters, journeymen and apprentices work under statutes.

models.name: Mercantilism
models.author: Thomas Mun
models.core: The state aims for a trade surplus, gold and colonies, and regulates production and trade to that end.
sources: Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade (1664)

models.name: Physiocracy
models.author: François Quesnay
models.core: Only agriculture creates a net product; a single tax on the rent of land should fund the state, and the grain trade should be free.

models.name: Classical laissez-faire capitalism
models.original: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
models.author: Adam Smith
models.core: Competitive markets, private property and the division of labour create wealth; the state protects property and contracts and otherwise stays out.

models.name: Austrian free-market economics
models.author: Carl Menger; Friedrich Hayek
models.core: Prices carry knowledge that is spread across many people and no planner can gather; state planning and credit expansion distort production.
sources: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)

models.name: Monetarist neoliberalism
models.author: Milton Friedman
models.core: Steady money growth, deregulation, privatisation and open trade, with a smaller state and fewer controls on markets.
sources: Harvey, A Brief History of Neoliberalism (2005)

models.name: Keynesian welfare capitalism
models.original: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
models.author: John Maynard Keynes
models.core: Government spending and taxes manage demand: they rise in slumps and fall in booms, so that employment stays high.
sources: Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services (1942)

models.name: Social market economy
models.author: Alfred Müller-Armack; Ludwig Erhard
models.core: Competitive markets operate inside a legal order that curbs monopoly, with social insurance and worker representation in firms.

models.name: Nordic social democracy
models.author: Swedish Social Democrats and trade unions
models.core: Universal public services and active labour-market policy, financed by high taxes, with strong unions and national wage bargaining.
sources: Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism (1990)

models.name: Developmental state
models.author: Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry
models.core: The state directs credit and export targets to chosen industries and disciplines firms by their performance.
sources: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982)

models.name: Georgism
models.author: Henry George
models.core: Tax the value of land rather than labour and capital, so that the rent of land funds public services and speculation in land falls.

models.name: Utopian socialism
models.author: Robert Owen; Charles Fourier
models.core: Cooperative communities and planned associations, built by example, replace wage competition and private profit.
sources: Owen, A New View of Society (1813)

models.name: Mutualism
models.author: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
models.core: Mutual credit and free contracts let workers keep the full value of their work; banks lend at cost and rent on property is abolished.

models.name: Cooperative economy
models.original: Rules of the Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers
models.author: Rochdale Pioneers
models.core: Members own and control firms and banks, one member one vote, and share the surplus between users and workers.

models.name: Anarcho-communism
models.author: Peter Kropotkin
models.core: No wages and no state; goods are shared according to need within federated communes, and free association replaces contracts.

models.name: Syndicalism
models.author: Fernand Pelloutier; the French CGT
models.core: Trade unions run industry directly through workers' organisations, using strikes and, eventually, a general strike.
sources: Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail (1902)

models.name: Fabian socialism
models.author: Sidney and Beatrice Webb
models.core: Socialism by democratic and gradual means: municipal and national public enterprise and a national minimum of welfare.

models.name: Guild socialism
models.author: G. D. H. Cole
models.core: Workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, with the state as one partner among several.

models.name: Command socialism
models.author: Soviet planners; Joseph Stalin
models.core: State ownership and central plans set output, prices and investment; the state mobilises labour for rapid industrialisation.

models.name: Market socialism
models.original: On the Economic Theory of Socialism
models.author: Oskar Lange; Fred Taylor
models.core: Public ownership with market prices, managers who follow prices, and a central board that sets the rules and the investment.
sources: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism (1938; Lange's essays date from 1936-1937)

models.name: Marxian communism
models.author: Karl Marx
models.core: After the state withers away and classes disappear, distribution follows the principle from each according to ability, to each according to need.
sources: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875)

models.name: Chinese market socialism
models.author: Deng Xiaoping and the Chinese leadership
models.core: Public ownership of key sectors alongside markets, special economic zones and gradual price reform under party direction.

models.name: Participatory economics
models.original: Looking Forward: Participatory Economics for the Twenty-First Century
models.author: Michael Albert; Robin Hahnel
models.core: Workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals; jobs are balanced in complexity; neither markets nor central planners allocate.

models.name: Corporatism and fascist economics
models.author: Benito Mussolini; Alfredo Rocco
models.core: Employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, and the state directs industry toward national goals, including war.

models.name: Islamic economics
models.author: Ahmad El Najjar
models.core: Interest (riba) is prohibited; finance shares profit and risk, zakat redistributes wealth, and trust underpins contracts.
sources: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System (1985)
Founding of the Mit Ghamr savings bank (1963)

models.name: Buddhist economics
models.author: E. F. Schumacher
models.core: Economic life serves well-being; consumption is moderate, and production is small-scale, local and non-violent.

models.name: Distributism
models.author: Pope Leo XIII; G. K. Chesterton; Hilaire Belloc
models.core: Widespread private property and small enterprise, a just wage, and subsidiarity so that decisions stay with the smallest competent body.

models.name: Steady-state and degrowth economics
models.author: Herman Daly; Kate Raworth
models.core: Economic activity stays within planetary limits, with no growth imperative and a social floor under everyone.

models.name: Universal basic income
models.author: Thomas Paine
models.core: Every citizen receives an unconditional income, paid for by taxes on land and natural resources.
sources: Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All (1995)

models.name: Modern monetary theory
models.author: Stephanie Kelton; L. Randall Wray
models.core: A government that issues its own currency can fund full employment; inflation, not debt, is the real limit.

models.name: Commons governance
models.author: Elinor Ostrom
models.core: Communities that share a resource govern it with rules they design, monitor and enforce, nested in wider institutions.
